s803.content:
Michaelina Hordashevska of Lviv took the name Josaphata when, in 1892, she became the first member of the Sister Servants of Mary Immaculate, the first active congregation of women in the Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church.

The sisters taught children, nursed the sick, and served the villages of Galicia. She died on April 7, 1919, after a painful illness, and John Paul II beatified her in Lviv in 2001.
s803.intercession: Blessed Josaphata, pray for us, and for the Church in Ukraine. Amen.

s804.content:
Francis Xavier Seelos, a Bavarian, came to the United States as a Redemptorist in 1843 and worked in Pittsburgh with St. John Neumann. He became a beloved confessor and preacher among immigrants across the country.

In New Orleans he nursed the victims of yellow fever, caught it himself, and died on October 4, 1867. John Paul II beatified him in 2000.
s804.intercession: Blessed Francis Xavier Seelos, pray for us, and for all immigrants. Amen.

s805.content:
Teresa Demjanovich was born in Bayonne, New Jersey, to Ruthenian immigrants and baptized in the Byzantine Catholic Church. She joined the Sisters of Charity of St. Elizabeth and taught at their academy.

At her director’s request she wrote spiritual conferences for the novices, published after her death as Greater Perfection. She died at twenty-six in 1927. Her beatification at Newark in 2014 was the first held in the United States.
s805.intercession: Blessed Miriam Teresa, pray for us. Teach us to seek holiness in ordinary things. Amen.

s806.content:
Felix, a priest of Nola near Naples, was imprisoned and tortured in the persecution of Decius. Later tradition tells that when he hid from his pursuers, a spider spun its web across the entrance and saved him.

He refused to be made bishop and died in peace. A century later St. Paulinus of Nola built a shrine at his tomb and wrote a poem for his feast every year.
s806.intercession: St. Felix, pray for us. Shelter us in time of danger. Amen.

s807.content:
Maurus was entrusted as a boy to St. Benedict and became his close disciple. St. Gregory the Great tells how, when young Placid fell into the lake at Subiaco, Benedict sent Maurus to save him, and Maurus ran out over the water without noticing, thinking only of obedience.

A later tradition says that he brought the Rule of St. Benedict to France. The 1962 calendar commemorates him on January 15.
s807.intercession: St. Maurus, pray for us. Teach us prompt obedience. Amen.

s808.content:
Aldhelm, a scholar of Wessex, became abbot of Malmesbury and in 705 the first bishop of Sherborne. He wrote learned Latin verse and prose, among the first of the English to do so.

King Alfred later recalled that Aldhelm also composed songs in English, and would stand on a bridge singing them to draw people in, then turn their attention to Scripture.
s808.intercession: St. Aldhelm, pray for us, and for poets and singers. Amen.

s809.content:
Theodore was a Greek monk from Tarsus, the city of St. Paul, living in Rome when Pope Vitalian chose him at sixty-six to be archbishop of Canterbury. He arrived in 669 with the abbot Hadrian.

He visited all of England, organized its dioceses, held the Synod of Hertford in 673, and with Hadrian founded a school at Canterbury where Greek and Latin were taught. He died in 690 at the age of eighty-eight.
s809.intercession: St. Theodore, pray for us, and for the Church in England. Amen.

s810.content:
Alphege was a monk who became bishop of Winchester and then, in 1006, archbishop of Canterbury. In 1011 Danish raiders sacked Canterbury and took him captive.

He refused to let a ransom be raised from his poor people, and on April 19, 1012, at Greenwich, his drunken captors pelted him with bones and killed him with an axe.
s810.intercession: St. Alphege, pray for us, and for all who suffer for others. Amen.

s811.content:
Wulfstan, a monk of Worcester, became its bishop in 1062 and was the only English bishop to keep his see for long after the Norman Conquest. He rebuilt his cathedral, visited his diocese tirelessly, and lived as simply as a monk.

He preached against the slave trade at Bristol, where men were sold to Ireland, until it ended. He was canonized in 1203.
s811.intercession: St. Wulfstan, pray for us, and for all who are enslaved. Amen.

s812.content:
Quadratus is the first Christian apologist whose name we know. When the Emperor Hadrian visited Athens around the year 125, Quadratus presented him with a written defense of the faith, so that the emperor would understand who the Christians were and stop listening to those who slandered them.

Only one sentence of it survives, quoted by Eusebius: the people Jesus healed and raised from the dead were not seen for a moment only, but remained, and some of them had lived into Quadratus’s own day. Tradition counts him a disciple of the apostles and a bishop of Athens.
s812.intercession: St. Quadratus, pray for us, that we may give a reason for the hope that is in us. Amen.

s813.content:
Aristides was a Christian philosopher of Athens who, like Quadratus, addressed a defense of the faith to the emperor in the second century. His Apology was lost for centuries, until a Syriac translation was found at St. Catherine’s Monastery on Mount Sinai in 1889.

In it he describes the Christians of his day: they do not commit adultery, they honor father and mother, they love their neighbors and do not take what is not theirs, and if one of them is poor and they have nothing to spare, they fast for two or three days to give him food.
s813.intercession: St. Aristides, pray for us, that our lives may show the beauty of the faith. Amen.

s814.content:
Apollinaris was bishop of Hierapolis in Phrygia in the second century, a successor of St. Papias. He was a learned writer who addressed an apology for the Christians to the Emperor Marcus Aurelius, and wrote against the pagans and the Jews of his time and against the Montanists, whose new “prophecy” was dividing the churches of Asia Minor.

His writings are lost, but Eusebius and others who read them held him in high esteem as one of the most eloquent defenders of the faith of his century.
s814.intercession: St. Apollinaris, pray for us, that we may hold fast to the faith of the apostles. Amen.

s815.content:
Dionysius was bishop of Corinth around the year 171, and one of the great letter writers of the early Church. He wrote to the churches of Rome, Athens, Crete, and elsewhere, encouraging them in faith and in charity, and warning them against error.

To Pope Soter he wrote that the Roman church read his letter aloud at the Sunday gathering, as it read the old letter of Clement, and he thanked the Romans for the alms they sent to Christians in need and in the mines. He is one of our earliest witnesses that Peter and Paul were both martyred in Rome.
s815.intercession: St. Dionysius, pray for us, and for the unity of all the churches. Amen.

s816.content:
Hegesippus was a Christian writer of the second century, perhaps a convert from Judaism, who traveled to Corinth and to Rome and made a list of the bishops of Rome down to his own day. He wanted to show that the true teaching had been handed on, unbroken, in every church from the apostles.

His five books of Memoirs are lost, but Eusebius drew on them for much of what we know of the earliest Church in Jerusalem, including the martyrdom of St. James, the brother of the Lord. He is sometimes called the father of Church history.
s816.intercession: St. Hegesippus, pray for us, that we may treasure what the apostles handed on. Amen.

s817.content:
Alexander was a student, with Origen, of the school of Alexandria, and a bishop in Cappadocia who was imprisoned for the faith. On a pilgrimage to Jerusalem around 212 he was asked to stay and help the aged bishop Narcissus, and he succeeded him.

He founded a library at Jerusalem, one of the first Christian libraries, which Eusebius later used to write his history. In the persecution of Decius he was taken to Caesarea and imprisoned again, and he died in chains in 251, an old man who had confessed Christ twice.
s817.intercession: St. Alexander, pray for us, and for all who keep books and learning. Amen.

s818.content:
Pamphilus was a priest of Caesarea in Palestine, and the greatest Bible scholar of his generation. He gathered and cared for the library left by Origen, and with his students copied the Scriptures with great care, comparing the manuscripts to correct their errors.

During the persecution of Diocletian he was arrested and kept in prison for two years, where he went on writing a defense of Origen, before he was beheaded with eleven companions in 309. His student Eusebius took the name “Eusebius of Pamphilus” in his honor.
s818.intercession: St. Pamphilus, pray for us, and for all who study and copy the word of God. Amen.

s819.content:
Victorinus was bishop of Poetovio, today Ptuj in Slovenia, and the first known writer to comment on the Scriptures in Latin. He wrote on many books of the Bible, and his commentary on the Book of Revelation is the oldest that survives.

He gave his life for Christ in the persecution of Diocletian, around 304. St. Jerome, who knew his writings, said that he spoke Greek better than Latin, and that what he wrote was great in meaning even when it was plain in style.
s819.intercession: St. Victorinus, pray for us, that we may love and understand the Scriptures. Amen.

s820.content:
Serapion was a monk of the Egyptian desert and a disciple of St. Anthony the Great, who left him one of his two sheepskins when he died. He became bishop of Thmuis in the Nile Delta, and stood beside St. Athanasius in the long struggle against Arianism, for which he was driven into exile.

Athanasius wrote him letters on the divinity of the Holy Spirit. A collection of prayers for the liturgy, the Euchologion of Serapion, has come down under his name, and St. Jerome called him “the Scholastic” for the learning of his writings.
s820.intercession: St. Serapion, pray for us, that we may glorify the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Amen.

s821.content:
Eusebius was bishop of Samosata on the Euphrates, and a friend of St. Basil the Great and St. Gregory of Nazianzus, who loved him dearly. In the years when the Arian emperor Valens persecuted the bishops who held to the faith of Nicaea, he traveled through Syria and Palestine in disguise, as a soldier, strengthening the churches and ordaining faithful bishops.

He was exiled to Thrace, and returned when Valens died. While installing a bishop in a town of his region, he was struck on the head by a tile thrown by an Arian woman, and died of the wound, forgiving her as he died.
s821.intercession: St. Eusebius, pray for us, that we may be faithful and forgiving. Amen.

s822.content:
Basil the Elder was a teacher of rhetoric in Pontus, and Emmelia the daughter of a martyr. They married and had nine or ten children, and five of them are honored as saints: Macrina the Younger, Basil the Great, Gregory of Nyssa, Peter of Sebaste, and Naucratius. Basil’s own mother was St. Macrina the Elder, a disciple of the disciples of St. Gregory the Wonderworker.

Basil died around 350. Emmelia, widowed, lived her last years in the community of prayer that her daughter Macrina gathered on the family estate at Annesi, and died around 375. Few families have given the Church so many saints.
s822.intercession: Sts. Basil and Emmelia, pray for all fathers and mothers, that they may raise their children for God. Amen.

s823.content:
Nonna was the wife of Gregory, a magistrate of Nazianzus in Cappadocia who belonged to a strange sect when they married. By her prayers and her example he became a Christian, and later bishop of Nazianzus.

She was the mother of St. Gregory the Theologian, St. Caesarius, and St. Gorgonia. Her son Gregory wrote of her that she prayed with tears, gave to the poor with a free hand, and never turned her back to the altar. She died in church, at prayer, in 374.
s823.intercession: St. Nonna, pray for all wives and mothers, and for the conversion of those they love. Amen.

s824.content:
Caesarius was the younger brother of St. Gregory of Nazianzus. He studied medicine at Alexandria and became one of the most famous physicians of his time, serving at the imperial court in Constantinople, where even the pagan emperor Julian tried in vain to win him away from the faith.

After surviving an earthquake at Nicaea, he resolved to give his life wholly to God, but he fell ill and died soon afterward, leaving everything to the poor. His brother’s funeral oration for him is one of the most moving of the age.
s824.intercession: St. Caesarius, pray for all physicians, that they may heal in the name of Christ. Amen.

s825.content:
Asterius was a lawyer who became bishop of Amasea in Pontus, in what is now Turkey, near the end of the fourth century. Many of his sermons survive, lively and full of the life of his city: he preached against the greed of the rich, the cruelty of divorce, and the luxury of clothes embroidered with Gospel scenes, telling his people to carry Christ in their hearts rather than on their garments.

His sermon on the martyr Euphemia, describing a painting of her death, was read aloud at the Second Council of Nicaea in 787 in defense of holy images.
s825.intercession: St. Asterius, pray for us, that we may carry Christ in our hearts. Amen.

s826.content:
Satyrus was the brother of St. Ambrose and St. Marcellina, born at Trier and trained as a lawyer in Rome. When Ambrose became bishop of Milan, Satyrus gave up his post as a provincial governor to manage the affairs of the church for him, so that his brother could give himself to prayer and preaching.

On a sea voyage he was shipwrecked, and he swam ashore carrying the Eucharist; soon afterward he was baptized. He died suddenly at Milan in 378, and Ambrose preached at his funeral the sermon On the Death of a Brother, full of grief and of hope in the resurrection.
s826.intercession: St. Satyrus, pray for us, and for all who serve the Church quietly. Amen.

s827.content:
Paulinus was a disciple of St. Maximin and succeeded him as bishop of Trier. At the Synod of Arles in 353, under pressure from the Arian emperor Constantius II, the bishops were told to condemn St. Athanasius; Paulinus alone refused.

He was exiled to Phrygia, far from his people, and passed from place to place among heretics and pagans until he died in exile in 358. His body was brought home to Trier in 395, and rests in the church that bears his name.
s827.intercession: St. Paulinus, pray for us, that we may stand by the truth when we stand alone. Amen.

s828.content:
Maximin came from near Poitiers and became the sixth bishop of Trier, then one of the capitals of the empire. When St. Athanasius was exiled from Alexandria, Maximin received him at Trier and gave him shelter for two years.

He defended the faith of Nicaea all his life and gave refuge to St. Paul of Constantinople as well. He died in 346, and his disciple St. Paulinus succeeded him.
s828.intercession: St. Maximin, pray for us, that we may welcome those who suffer for the truth. Amen.

s829.content:
Victricius was the son of a Roman soldier and became a soldier himself, until, as a Christian, he laid down his arms and refused to fight, for which he was flogged and condemned, though in the end released.

He became bishop of Rouen around 393 and preached the Gospel in the countryside of northern Gaul, founding monasteries and receiving relics of the saints with great joy; his sermon In Praise of the Saints survives. He was a friend of St. Martin of Tours and St. Paulinus of Nola, and traveled to Britain to make peace among its bishops.
s829.intercession: St. Victricius, pray for us, and for all soldiers who seek to follow Christ. Amen.

s830.content:
Honoratus was a young nobleman of Gaul who gave up his wealth and, after a pilgrimage, settled with a few companions on the island of Lérins, off the coast of Provence, around 410. The monastery that grew there became one of the great schools of saints in the West: bishops, writers, and monks came from it for generations.

In 426 he was made bishop of Arles, and he died there in 429. His kinsman and disciple St. Hilary of Arles, who succeeded him, wrote his life and remembered his kindness, which drew people to God as much as his teaching.
s830.intercession: St. Honoratus, pray for us, that we may find God in silence and prayer. Amen.

s831.content:
Lupus was a lawyer who, seven years into his marriage, agreed with his wife to live as brother and sister, and became a monk at Lérins. Around 426 he was made bishop of Troyes, and he governed it for more than fifty years.

With St. Germanus of Auxerre he traveled to Britain in 429 to defend the faith against the Pelagians. When Attila and the Huns came toward Troyes in 451, Lupus went out to meet him, and the city was spared.
s831.intercession: St. Lupus, pray for us, and for all who must face danger for their people. Amen.

s832.content:
Sidonius was a poet and statesman of the Gallo-Roman nobility, the son-in-law of an emperor and prefect of the city of Rome. In 469 he was chosen bishop of Clermont in Auvergne, and he gave himself to his new flock, giving the family silver to the poor.

As the Western Empire fell he led the defense of Clermont against the Visigoths. When the city was handed over he was imprisoned for a time, then returned to his people. His letters and poems are one of our best windows onto the world of late Roman Gaul.
s832.intercession: St. Sidonius, pray for us, that we may serve God in every change of fortune. Amen.

s833.content:
Avitus came from a senatorial family of Gaul and became bishop of Vienne around 490. He worked patiently to bring the Burgundian kings, who were Arians, to the Catholic faith, and King Sigismund was converted through him.

He was also a poet: his long Latin poem on the creation, the fall, and the flood is one of the finest of its age. He wrote a famous letter to Clovis, king of the Franks, rejoicing at his baptism.
s833.intercession: St. Avitus, pray for us, and for all who work for the conversion of those in power. Amen.

s834.content:
Ennodius was a nobleman of Gaul raised in Italy, a poet and teacher of rhetoric who became a deacon of Milan and then, in 514, bishop of Pavia. Many of his letters, poems, and speeches survive.

Pope Hormisdas twice sent him to Constantinople to work for the end of the schism between Rome and the Church of the East, and though his missions did not succeed, his patience prepared the reconciliation that came soon after his death in 521.
s834.intercession: St. Ennodius, pray for us, and for the unity of the Church. Amen.

s835.content:
Petronius came of a noble Roman family and became bishop of Bologna in the fifth century. He rebuilt the city after its devastation and built there the church of Santo Stefano, a group of chapels meant to recall the holy places of Jerusalem.

He is the patron of Bologna, and its great basilica, one of the largest churches in the world, bears his name.
s835.intercession: St. Petronius, pray for us, and for the city where we live. Amen.

s836.content:
Aurelius was bishop of Carthage from about 391 until his death, and so the leading bishop of Christian Africa in the age of St. Augustine, who was his close friend. He called and presided over many councils of the African Church, which settled questions of discipline and of the books of Scripture.

With Augustine he defended the faith against the Donatists and the Pelagians, and he encouraged the founding of monasteries.
s836.intercession: St. Aurelius, pray for us, and for all who lead the Church in councils. Amen.

s837.content:
Alypius was St. Augustine’s friend from childhood in Thagaste, and his student. Augustine tells in his Confessions how Alypius was drawn into the bloody games of the arena, and freed from them. He was with Augustine in the garden at Milan when Augustine heard the words “Take up and read,” and he too gave himself to Christ; they were baptized together by St. Ambrose in 387.

He shared Augustine’s life of prayer in Africa and became bishop of their home town, Thagaste, around 394, working beside his friend all his life.
s837.intercession: St. Alypius, pray for us, and for all true friends who lead each other to God. Amen.

s838.content:
Quodvultdeus, whose name means “what God wills,” was a deacon of Carthage who corresponded with St. Augustine and became bishop of Carthage. When the Vandals, who were Arians, took the city in 439, King Gaiseric put him and many of his clergy on old ships without sails or oars and set them adrift.

They came safely to Naples, where Quodvultdeus died in exile. Several of his sermons survive.
s838.intercession: St. Quodvultdeus, pray for us, that we may accept what God wills. Amen.

s839.content:
Gregory was bishop of Elvira, near today’s Granada in Spain, in the fourth century. He was one of the most unbending defenders of the faith of Nicaea, refusing to accept the compromise creed of the Council of Rimini in 359 when many bishops gave way.

Several of his writings survive, including a treatise on the faith against the Arians and sermons on the Scriptures, among them commentaries on the Song of Songs.
s839.intercession: St. Gregory, pray for us, that we may hold to the true faith without compromise. Amen.

s840.content:
Braulio was a student of St. Isidore of Seville and became bishop of Zaragoza in 631. He was the most learned bishop of Visigothic Spain after Isidore, whose great Etymologies he edited and divided into the books we know.

His letters survive, and his life of the hermit St. Emilian. He took a leading part in the councils of Toledo, and was known for his kindness to the poor.
s840.intercession: St. Braulio, pray for us, and for all students and teachers. Amen.

s841.content:
Fructuosus was the son of a Visigothic noble who gave away his inheritance and became a hermit in the mountains of northwestern Spain. So many followed him that he founded monastery after monastery, and wrote rules for them; one of his foundations was a double monastery so large that the king feared the army would be emptied.

He was made abbot-bishop of Dumio and then archbishop of Braga, and he died in 665. His life was written soon after his death.
s841.intercession: St. Fructuosus, pray for us, and for all who seek God in solitude. Amen.

s842.content:
Julian was born in Toledo, studied at its cathedral school, and became a monk and a disciple of St. Eugene. In 680 he was made archbishop of Toledo and primate of all Spain, and he presided over four councils.

He was the leading theologian of Visigothic Spain. His Prognosticon, a work on death, the soul after death, and the resurrection, was read across Europe for centuries.
s842.intercession: St. Julian, pray for us, that we may prepare well for death and the life to come. Amen.
